title: POC Planning — Capacity & Fallbacks (Apex Analytics)
next_steps: Maya to send 3-month reserved GPU pricing + burst credit options by 2025-12-09
SE to share benchmark harness and sample payloads (oss link) by 2025-12-10
Schedule 60-min benchmark kickoff with Apex infra (target 2025-12-12)
action_items: Maya: Draft commercial proposal for 3x A100 reserved + 2x burst slots — due 2025-12-09
Diego: Prepare benchmark harness repo and run sample 10k-token profile — due 2025-12-10
Anita: Share internal traffic profile (qps, seq len distribution) and security checklist — due 2025-12-09
summary: Discovery / POC scoping focused on sizing a reserved GPU pool and defining burst and fallback policies. Apex wants predictable tail latency for low-latency responder use cases and tight cost controls. Agreement to run a benchmark with their traffic profile and validate fallback to quantized model variants under heavy load.
questions: What are absolute latency SLOs by route?
How do we measure graceful degradation (quality vs latency)?
Which model variants are acceptable for fallback?
transcript:
00:00:00 - Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're looking to scope the POC around capacity sizing and autoscale patterns for Apex's inference needs. Goal today is define success criteria and concrete bench steps.
00:00:12 - Lucy Park: Thanks, Maya. Quick context: we run an analytics assistant that serves sub-second answers for our dashboard queries, but we also have long-form generation for reports. Latency tail concerns are mostly for the dashboard path.
00:00:40 - Tom Blake: Right — main ask is keep p95 under 350ms for dashboard-ish calls at 30 qps sustained, with short spikes to ~120 qps during batch refresh.
00:01:05 - Diego Rivera: Got it. Are those requests short tokens or do you have a distribution?
00:01:12 - Lucy Park: Mostly short, 16–64 tokens for prompts, but the report path can be 1k–5k tokens and runs asynchronously. We can share the histograms after this call.
00:01:30 - Anita Rao: One constraint — data residency and KMS-integrated keys, plus we need audit logs for every inference call for a compliance bucket.
00:01:45 - Maya Chen: That's standard — Redwood Private options, or Dedicated with customer VPC peering and KMS integration. We'll include audit log retention options in the checklist.
00:02:10 - Tom Blake: Costs — we have a budget for the POC but want a path to predictable unit economics if we go to production.
00:02:20 - Diego Rivera: For the sizing exercise I generally map short-path qps to per-GPU sustained throughput. For example, an A100 v8-style reserved pool can handle roughly X short-requests per second depending on batching and KV cache hit rate. Do you currently use KV cache or prefix caching in your stack?
00:02:45 - Lucy Park: No KV cache today, it's all naive calls behind our API. That's something we can add.
00:02:55 - Diego Rivera: Ok, that'll materially reduce token compute. For the POC we recommend: 3x reserved GPUs for baseline, plus 2 burst slots that can spin up for 15–30 minute windows. Fallback policy: when capacity saturated, fall back to a smaller quantized model that preserves semantics for short-answer routes.
00:03:25 - Anita Rao: How do you ensure quality when falling back to a quantized variant? We can't have hallucination spikes when traffic is high.
00:03:35 - Samir Patel: Great question — part of the POC is to run parallel A/B benchmarks: run full model and quantized variant on a representative prompt set and compare key metrics (perplexity, exact-match for structured outputs, user-facing downstream diffs). We'll attach an eval harness.
00:03:58 - Tom Blake: We care about the tail — under heavy load, the product can't degrade into timeouts. So fallback needs to be deterministic and predictable, not just "best effort".
00:04:12 - Diego Rivera: Agreed. Our recommended fallback chain: 1) route to idle capacity within region (reserved pool spare), 2) burst capacity (pre-warmed G PUs), 3) fallback model variant (quantized L2/INT8), 4) last-resort: degraded response with partial result and explicit "truncated due to load" marker. Each step has a soft SLO and observable metric.
00:04:45 - Lucy Park: That last-resort truncated marker is critical — we want the frontend to show a banner instead of hanging.
00:04:55 - Maya Chen: We'll include examples of the response envelope that includes fallback_reason and model_version.
00:05:10 - Tom Blake: What's the expected cost delta for keeping 2 burst slots vs just scaling reserved up?
00:05:18 - Diego Rivera: Depends on burst duration. If bursts are infrequent (a few 10–20 minute windows per day), having burst credits with a smaller reserved baseline is cheaper. If you have sustained load above baseline, reserved capacity is cheaper. We'll model a 30-day cost projection in the proposal.
00:05:40 - Anita Rao: On security: SSO and SCIM provision, KMS for model keys, and we need to confirm where logs are stored. Are audit logs in plaintext or can they be tokenized?
00:05:55 - Samir Patel: We have options — full audit trail to your S3 (encrypted), or Redwood-managed storage with encryption-at-rest and customer-supplied KMS. We'll share the SOC2/ISO artefacts.
00:06:18 - Lucy Park: Let's talk benchmarks specifics — what metrics, and what's the harness?
00:06:25 - Diego Rivera: We'll run two harnesses: 1) latency focused — synthetic QPS at short token lengths to validate p95/p99; 2) throughput/long-tail generator — long token sessions simulated to check GPU memory/KV cache behavior. Metrics: latency distributions, effective tokens/sec, GPU utilization, cache hit rate, model quality diffs, and cost per 1k tokens.
00:06:52 - Tom Blake: Can you run the harness against our internal VPC if we provide credentials? Data can't leave our environment for now.
00:06:58 - Maya Chen: Yes, we can run the Redwood Private package or spin up a Dedicated trial in your cloud account. For quick iteration we sometimes do a shared-hosted benchmark with sanitized payloads, but for compliance we'll run in your VPC.
00:07:20 - Anita Rao: Timeline — we want results before end of year. Is that feasible?
00:07:26 - Maya Chen: Tight but doable. Proposed plan: this week share harness + payload samples (Apex), next week run initial short-latency benchmark, then week after run mixed-load with fallback tests. Final report within 2 weeks of the runs.
00:07:44 - Diego Rivera: For the run we'll need: traffic histogram, sample prompts, target SLOs per route, and a list of acceptable fallback variants.
00:07:55 - Lucy Park: We'll share histograms and a small labeled eval set for quality checks by EOD Tuesday.
00:08:04 - Tom Blake: Are there any licensing or IP concerns with running our data in a Redwood-managed harness?
00:08:10 - Maya Chen: We'll use sanitized or customer-managed harness in your VPC where data never leaves. Contractually we'll put the usual protections in the pilot MSA.
00:08:26 - Jared - procurement: Pricing questions: if we commit to 3-month reserved, is there an early-termination adjustment?
00:08:34 - Maya Chen: Yes, our reserved terms have a prorated early-termination clause for pilots; I'll include the specific schedule in the commercial draft.
00:08:45 - Anita Rao: Operationally, how do you do autoscaling with short-latency targets? Spinning GPUs up can be slow.
00:08:54 - Samir Patel: We employ pre-warmed burst slots and fast checkpoint restore optimizations. Autoscaler policy is workload-aware: if traffic has predictable diurnal patterns we keep warm capacity; for sudden spikes we route to burst then fallback. Latency-sensitive routes are pinned to reserved capacity where possible.
00:09:20 - Diego Rivera: Also caching: prefix/KV cache avoids re-encoding prompt tokens and reduces per-request latency; in practice we've seen 20–40% p95 improvements on chatty workloads.
00:09:33 - Lucy Park: If we add KV cache, we need eviction and consistency guarantees across region replicas.
00:09:40 - Diego Rivera: We can configure strong or eventual semantics depending on the use case; we'll include recommended config.
00:09:50 - Tom Blake: Benchmarks: include tests that intentionally saturate reserved pool to validate fallback policies and that fallback doesn't blow up quality.
00:09:58 - Diego Rivera: Absolutely; we'll run a step test where we ramp to 200% baseline and verify routing to burst and then model switchovers, capture QoS metrics and diffs.
00:10:12 - Maya Chen: Ok recap: Maya to send pricing and pilot commercial; Diego/Samir send harness + run plan; Apex to share traffic profiles and eval set. We agreed on 3 reserved GPUs baseline + 2 burst slots recommendation, subject to benchmark results.
00:10:34 - Lucy Park: One more practical: what's the smallest quantized model you support for fallback? We need something that keeps entity extraction and few-shot prompts intact.
00:10:44 - Samir Patel: We support INT8 quantized variants of our supported models and have tuned post-quantization calibration for extraction tasks. We'll include quality deltas on the eval.
00:10:58 - Tom Blake: Who will own the run on Redwood side?
00:11:03 - Maya Chen: Diego will be the technical lead; Maya AE on commercial. We'll loop in Samir for ops.
00:11:12 - Anita Rao: Is there a sandbox where we can preview the response structure with fallback fields?
00:11:18 - Diego Rivera: Yes — we'll push an example schema and a tiny demo endpoint you can hit.
00:11:25 - Jared - procurement: Please include line items for burst credits and overage, we need that for procurement sign-off.
00:11:32 - Maya Chen: Will do.
00:11:35 - Lucy Park: Ok great, thanks — excited to see the bench results.
00:11:40 - Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with artifacts.
00:11:46 - [End of meeting — recording stops]
notes: Apex wants p95 < 350ms for dashboard route at 30 qps baseline; spikes to 120 qps.
Recommended starting config: 3x reserved GPUs + 2 burst slots; fallback chain documented.
Benchmark plan: latency harness + mixed-load generator + quality eval set.
